content: Neotyphodium is a form genus that includes species of endophytic fungi. These endophytes are asexual, seed-borne symbionts that inhabit cool-season grasses. They grow intercellularly throughout the aerial tissues of their host plants, including shoot apical meristems, leaf sheaths and blades, inflorescences, seeds, and embryos. Molecular phylogenetic evidence indicates that asexual Neotyphodium species are derived either from individual Epichloë species or, more commonly, from hybrids involving at least two ancestral Epichloë species. Consequently, the form genus Neotyphodium is closely associated with the teleomorphic genus Epichloë. According to the botanical nomenclature code, the form genus refers to the asexual spore or vegetative state, while the teleomorphic genus refers to the sexual state. Neotyphodium fungi infect new grass plants exclusively by growing into the seeds of their grass hosts and subsequently infecting the developing seedlings. In contrast, the sexual state, which occurs only in Epichloë fungi, leads to a condition known as choke disease. This disease is characterized by the fungal overgrowth engulfing grass inflorescences, forming a stroma and preventing seed production. Effects on Grass Plants and Herbivores It has been hypothesized that vertically transmitted symbionts, such as Neotyphodium, should evolve to be mutualistic because their reproductive success is closely tied to that of their hosts. Indeed, Neotyphodium species confer several benefits to their host plants, including enhanced growth, improved drought tolerance, and increased resistance to herbivores and pathogens. Resistance to herbivores is attributed to alkaloids produced by the endophytes. While grass-endophyte symbioses are widely recognized as mutualistic in many wild and cultivated grasses, the interactions can vary significantly and may even become antagonistic under nutrient-poor soil conditions. Neotyphodium Alkaloids Neotyphodium endophytes produce several classes of alkaloids with biological activity against herbivores, including mammals and insects. 1. Ergoline Alkaloids: These are ergot alkaloids, named after the ergot fungus Claviceps purpurea, a close relative of Neotyphodium and Epichloë. Ergoline alkaloids are characterized by a ring system derived from 4-prenyl tryptophan. One of the most abundant ergoline alkaloids in endophyte-symbiotic grasses is ergovaline, which consists of an ergoline moiety attached to a bicyclic tripeptide containing the amino acids L-proline, L-alanine, and L-valine. 2. Indole-Diterpenoid Alkaloids: These include compounds such as lolitrem B, which exhibit biological activity against mammalian herbivores and some insects. 3. Peramine: This is a pyrrolopyrazine alkaloid thought to be biosynthesized from the guanidinium-group-containing amino acid L-arginine and pyrrolidine-5-carboxylate, a precursor of L-proline. Peramine acts as an insect-feeding deterrent. 4. Loline Alkaloids: These are 1-aminopyrrolizidines with an oxygen atom linking the bridgehead carbons 2 and 7. They are biosynthesized from the amino acids L-proline and L-homoserine. Loline alkaloids exhibit insecticidal and insect-deterrent activities comparable to nicotine. Many, but not all, Neotyphodium species produce up to three classes of these alkaloids, which contribute to their ecological roles and interactions with host plants and herbivores.
